pharm: Mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 (IDH1) inhibitor; lowers oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) and restores myeloid cell differentiation
tags: Relapsed or refractory AML with IDH1 mutation
quick: On an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal
Can cause fetal harm; avoid - use effective contraception
Do not breastfeed during and for 2 weeks after the last dose
No adjustment defined; limited data in severe impairment - monitor closely
Monitor liver tests; hold or reduce for hepatotoxicity; limited data in severe impairment
No specific interaction; limit due to additive hepatic effects
Differentiation syndrome signs, liver tests, ECG/QTc and electrolytes, CBC
summary: Olutasidenib (Rezlidhia) is an oral mutant IDH1 inhibitor for adults with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia with a susceptible IDH1 mutation detected by an FDA-approved test. The dose is 150 mg twice daily on an empty stomach until progression or unacceptable toxicity. It carries a boxed warning for differentiation syndrome, which can be fatal and requires prompt corticosteroids, hemodynamic monitoring, and drug interruption. Other key risks are hepatotoxicity, QTc prolongation, and embryo-fetal toxicity. It is a CYP3A substrate, so strong or moderate CYP3A inducers should be avoided.
indications: Treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with a susceptible IDH1 mutation as detected by an FDA-approved test

dosage.c: Relapsed or refractory AML with susceptible IDH1 mutation
dosage.n: Continue until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity; in the absence of progression or toxicity, treat for at least 6 months to allow time for response
dosage.t: Twice daily, about 12 hours apart, on an empty stomach

dosage.d: Withhold olutasidenib until signs and symptoms improve
dosage.n: Give systemic corticosteroids and hemodynamic monitoring until resolution and for at least 3 days; resume at 150 mg twice daily after resolution and manage recurrence the same way

dosage.d: Withhold, then resume at the same or a reduced dose per labeling based on severity and recurrence
dosage.n: Permanently discontinue for severe or recurrent life-threatening hepatic or cardiac toxicity

admin: Take 150 mg by mouth twice daily, about 12 hours apart, on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal)
Swallow capsules whole with water; do not open, crush, chew, or dissolve
Take at the same times each day until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity; allow at least 6 months without progression before judging lack of response

If differentiation syndrome is suspected (fever, dyspnea, hypoxia, rash, edema, rapid weight gain, hypotension), hold drug and seek urgent care; treatment is systemic corticosteroids with hemodynamic monitoring
Obtain baseline and periodic ECG, electrolytes, liver tests, and blood counts during therapy
moa: Olutasidenib is a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 (IDH1). Mutant IDH1 converts alpha-ketoglutarate to the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which blocks normal myeloid differentiation. Olutasidenib lowers 2-HG levels and restores differentiation of leukemic blasts. It is active against susceptible IDH1 variants (most commonly R132 substitutions) in relapsed or refractory AML.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity to olutasidenib or any excipient
monitor: Signs of differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, hypoxia, rash, weight gain, edema, hypotension)
Liver tests and symptoms of hepatotoxicity (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, dark urine)
Blood counts and pregnancy status before starting
relative: Pre-existing QT prolongation, relevant cardiac disease, or use of QT-prolonging drugs
Concomitant strong or moderate CYP3A inducers (reduced exposure)

preg: Based on its mechanism and animal findings, olutasidenib can cause fetal harm. Verify pregnancy status before starting in females of reproductive potential and advise effective contraception during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose.
lact: There are no data on olutasidenib in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose.
renal: No dose adjustment is defined for renal impairment. There are limited data in severe renal impairment; use with caution and monitor closely for adverse reactions.
hepatic: Monitor liver tests before starting and at least monthly; dose interruption, reduction, or discontinuation may be needed for hepatotoxicity. Olutasidenib has not been well studied in severe hepatic impairment; use with caution and monitor closely.

interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction is described; limit alcohol because of additive liver and constitutional effects.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor liver tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase), ECG (QTc), potassium and magnesium, complete blood counts, and pregnancy status.
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal); food effects on absorption are addressed by this fasting requirement.
major: Strong or moderate CYP3A inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) - substantially reduce olutasidenib exposure; avoid
QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., certain antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, methadone) - additive QTc risk; avoid or monitor ECG and electrolytes closely
minor: Gastric acid-reducing agents have no major described effect on dosing; follow administration instructions
moderate: Sensitive CYP1A2 substrates with a narrow therapeutic index - olutasidenib may alter their exposure; monitor for effect and adjust as needed

emergency: Fever with dyspnea, hypoxia, rash, rapid weight gain, swelling, or hypotension (differentiation syndrome) - seek emergency care
Syncope, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat (QT prolongation/arrhythmia)
Jaundice, severe right upper quadrant pain, or dark urine with marked fatigue (hepatotoxicity)
serious: Differentiation syndrome, which can be fatal (boxed warning)
Hepatotoxicity with transaminase and bilirubin elevation

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of differentiation syndrome for weeks to months after starting, including with or without leukocytosis
Liver tests before starting and at least monthly, with prompt evaluation of transaminase or bilirubin rises
ECG for QTc and serum potassium and magnesium at baseline and periodically
Complete blood counts and clinical response; pregnancy status before starting in females of reproductive potential
counsel: This drug carries a boxed warning for differentiation syndrome, which can be fatal: report fever, trouble breathing, rash, swelling, rapid weight gain, dizziness, or low blood pressure right away
Take on an empty stomach as directed; if you vomit or miss a dose, skip it and take the next dose at the regular time - do not take two doses together
Report yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, right-sided belly pain, unusual tiredness, fainting, or palpitations
Use effective contraception during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose; do not breastfeed during and for 2 weeks after the last dose
Tell your team about all medicines, especially seizure medicines, rifampin-like antibiotics, St John's wort, and drugs that affect heart rhythm
pk: 2-HG reduction within days; hematologic responses develop over weeks to months
Median plasma Tmax about 4 hours after oral dosing
Steady state reached in about 2 weeks with twice-daily dosing; effect persists for days after stopping
Store at 20-25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted); keep in original container, protect from moisture
pearls: Boxed warning: differentiation syndrome, which can be fatal - hold drug plus corticosteroids and hemodynamic monitoring at the first suspicion
Take on an empty stomach twice daily; allow at least 6 months without progression before concluding lack of benefit
Hepatotoxicity and QTc prolongation require scheduled liver tests, ECG, and electrolyte monitoring
CYP3A substrate - avoid strong or moderate CYP3A inducers because of loss of efficacy
Embryo-fetal toxicity - confirm contraception during and for 2 weeks after treatment; do not breastfeed
missed: If a dose is missed or vomited, skip it and take the next dose at the regularly scheduled time. Do not take two doses together to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for olutasidenib overdose. Manage with supportive care, including cardiac monitoring (ECG for QT prolongation), electrolyte correction, liver tests, and observation for differentiation syndrome. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
